item.title: Docker networks
item.description:
Docker provides several built-in network drivers to handle container communication, isolation, and routing. Each driver serves a specific architectural use case depending on whether containers run on a single host, across multiple hosts, or require direct physical network integration.

1. Bridge Network (Default)

The bridge network creates a software switch on the host (usually named docker0). Containers attached to the same bridge can communicate with each other via internal IP addresses.

  • Default Bridge: Automatically assigned to containers if no network is specified. Does not support automatic DNS resolution by container name; containers must communicate via IP or manual --link.
  • User-Defined Bridge: Custom bridge created with docker network create -d bridge <name>. Provides automatic service discovery (DNS resolution via container names) and better isolation.
  • Best used for: Standalone containers running on a single host needing private, isolated inter-container communication. Bash
# Create and run on a user-defined bridge
docker network create my-bridge
docker run -d --name web --network my-bridge nginx
docker run -it --network my-bridge alpine ping web

2. Host Network

The host driver removes network isolation between the container and the Docker host. The container shares the host’s networking namespace directly.

  • Port Behavior: Port mapping (-p or -P) is ignored. If a service in the container binds to port 80, it immediately binds to port 80 on the host machine.
  • Performance: Eliminates Network Address Translation (NAT) overhead, achieving near-native network throughput.
  • Limitations: Only works natively on Linux hosts (on macOS and Windows, Docker runs inside a lightweight VM, so the host network attaches to the VM rather than your actual OS).
  • Best used for: High-throughput, low-latency applications (e.g., media streaming, high-frequency trading) or services monitoring the host’s network stack. Bash
docker run -d --name cache --network host redis

3. None Network

The none driver disables all networking for the container.

  • Configuration: The container only receives a loopback interface (127.0.0.1 / ::1). No external interfaces, gateway, or routing table are created.
  • Best used for: Completely air-gapped tasks, batch jobs running untrusted code, or containers generating local cryptographic keys where external connectivity poses a security risk. Bash
docker run -it --network none alpine ifconfig

4. Overlay Network

The overlay driver manages multi-host networking by encapsulating Layer 2 Ethernet frames inside Layer 4 UDP packets (VXLAN tunnels) across different Docker daemon hosts.

  • Scope: Requires Docker Swarm mode or an external key-value store (like Consul/etcd) to sync routing tables across nodes.
  • DNS & Routing: Provides automatic multi-host service discovery and ingress routing (routing mesh), distributing traffic across Swarm replicas automatically.
  • Best used for: Multi-host orchestration, Swarm clusters, and distributed container systems without third-party network plugins. Bash
# Swarm must be initialized first: docker swarm init
docker network create -d overlay --attachable my-overlay

5. Macvlan Network

The macvlan driver assigns a distinct physical MAC address to each container, making them appear as physical devices directly attached to the host’s local network router.

  • Subnet Integration: Containers obtain routable IP addresses directly from the local LAN’s DHCP server or a dedicated subnet.
  • Host Caveat: By default, Linux kernel routing prevents communication directly between the Docker host and its own macvlan containers.
  • Best used for: Legacy enterprise applications requiring direct Layer 2 connectivity, network monitoring tools, or setups where external network firewalls inspect container traffic by IP/MAC address. Bash
docker network create -d macvlan \
--subnet=192.168.1.0/24 \
--gateway=192.168.1.1 \
-o parent=eth0 my-macvlan

6. Ipvlan Network

Similar to macvlan, the ipvlan driver provides direct Layer 2/Layer 3 network integration, but all containers share the parent interface’s physical MAC address while maintaining distinct IP addresses.

  • Modes:
    • L2 Mode: Operates like a switch; containers share the host MAC but have individual IPs. Requires standard ARP resolution.
      • L3 Mode: Operates as a router; eliminates broadcast traffic, ARP, and Layer 2 switching. The Docker host routes traffic between subnets.
  • Best used for: Networks with strict MAC address limits (e.g., public cloud hypervisors, switches with port security enabled) or high-density container deployments where ARP storms must be avoided. Bash
docker network create -d ipvlan \
--subnet=192.168.20.0/24 \
--gateway=192.168.20.1 \
-o ipvlan_mode=l2 \
-o parent=eth0 my-ipvlan

7. Network Plugins (Third-Party / CNI)

Docker supports third-party networking extensions via the Container Network Interface (CNI) or custom Docker network plugins.

  • Examples: Calico, Weave Net, Cilium, Flannel.
  • Features: Advanced capabilities such as BGP routing, eBPF data planes, cross-cluster wireguard encryption, and fine-grained network policies/firewalls.
  • Best used for: Production Kubernetes migrations, regulated environments needing micro-segmentation, and cloud-native service meshes.

Driver Comparison

Driver Host Scope Multi-Host? Performance Automatic DNS? Common Use Case
Bridge Single No Good (NAT overhead) Yes (User-defined only) Standard web stacks, local microservices
Host Single No Maximum (Native) Host-dependent High performance, raw port binding
None Single No N/A None Air-gapped batch jobs, security sandboxing
Overlay Multi Yes Moderate (VXLAN encapsulation) Yes Docker Swarm, multi-node setups
Macvlan Single/LAN Direct to LAN High Router-dependent Legacy migrations, VLAN compliance
Ipvlan Single/LAN Direct to LAN High Router-dependent High-density networks, MAC-restricted switches

item.title: Kubernetes
item.description:
Kubernetes (K8s) is a distributed control system designed around a single architectural axiom: declarative state management executed via continuous reconciliation loops. Instead of executing imperative run commands, you declare a target topology, and an array of autonomous, decoupled controllers constantly work to converge the cluster’s actual state to that declared state.

1. Control Plane Architecture: The State & Decision Engine

The control plane coordinates cluster logic, enforces policies, and holds persistent state.

+-------------------------------------------------------+
| Control Plane |
| |
kubectl ----> | [kube-apiserver] <-------> [etcd (Raft Quorum)] |
| ^ |
| |-- [kube-controller-manager] (Reconciliation)|
| |-- [kube-scheduler] (Filter -> Score) |
+---------|---------------------------------------------+
| Watch API (HTTP/2 gRPC Streams)
+------------------+------------------+
| |
v v
+--------------------------+ +--------------------------+
| Worker Node 1 | | Worker Node 2 |
| [kubelet] -> CRI runtime | | [kubelet] -> CRI runtime |
| [kube-proxy] (iptables/ | | [kube-proxy] (iptables/ |
| IPVS/eBPF) | | IPVS/eBPF) |
| Pod (veth / netns) | | Pod (veth / netns) |
+--------------------------+ +--------------------------+

etcd: The Canonical Source of Truth

  • Mechanism: A consistent, distributed key-value store using the Raft consensus algorithm.
  • Storage Schema: Keys are stored hierarchically (e.g., /registry/pods/<namespace>/<pod-name>). It maintains a monotonically increasing 64-bit counter called a ResourceVersion (backed by Raft commit indices and bbolt b-trees).
  • Isolation: Only kube-apiserver communicates directly with etcd. No other component (kubelet, scheduler, etc.) ever reads or writes to etcd directly.

kube-apiserver: The Gateway & State Serializer

The API server is stateless, scales horizontally behind a layer-4 load balancer, and exposes a RESTful JSON/Protobuf HTTP/2 API. When an incoming payload arrives, it runs through a strict linear pipeline:

  1. Authentication: Decodes bearer tokens, X.509 client certs, or OIDC claims to establish User, Groups, and Extra.
  2. Authorization: Checks privileges via RBAC (Role-Based Access Control), ABAC, or Webhook authorizers.
  3. Mutating Admission Webhooks: Invokes webhooks to modify payloads (e.g., injecting sidecars or default resource requests).
  4. Schema Validation: Verifies syntax, required fields, and structural specifications against the OpenAPI schema.
  5. Validating Admission Webhooks: Runs policy validation (e.g., OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno) to reject non-compliant specs.
  6. Persistence: Commits to etcd and assigns a new ResourceVersion.
  7. Watch Distribution: Streams changes via long-lived HTTP/2 streams (watch) to listeners using the Reflector mechanism inside client-go.

kube-controller-manager: The Reconciliation Engine

Runs dozens of discrete control loops inside a single process. A controller implements the level-triggered reconciliation loop:

INI8 Labs

Reconcile():Actual State→ΔDesired State \text{Reconcile}() : \quad \text{Actual State} \xrightarrow{\quad\Delta\quad} \text{Desired State} Reconcile():Actual StateΔ​Desired State

Using client-go Informer and Lister patterns, controllers cache state locally to avoid overloading kube-apiserver. When an event occurs, an informer pushes the key into a WorkQueue, and worker threads pop the key, calculate delta, and post patch requests back to the API server.

  • DeploymentController reconciles Deployment \rightarrow creates/updates ReplicaSet. INI8 Labs
  • ReplicaSetController reconciles ReplicaSet →\rightarrow→ creates/updates raw Pod manifests.
  • NodeController tracks node heartbeats (Leases) and evicts pods when nodes become NotReady. INI8 Labs

kube-scheduler: Algorithmic Placement

Monitors pods where spec.nodeName == "". Placement runs in a two-phase cycle:

  1. Filtering (Predicates): Prunes ineligible nodes (e.g., checks resource requests vs. node allocatable capacity, node selectors, taints/tolerations, port collisions, volume zone topology).
  2. Scoring (Priorities): Assigns a 0–100 score across remaining nodes based on weighted rules (e.g., image locality, inter-pod anti-affinity spreading, balanced resource allocation).
  3. Binding: Atomically updates the pod’s spec.nodeName via a /binding subresource call to kube-apiserver.

2. Worker Node Architecture: The Execution Engine

Worker nodes run the scheduled containers and manage the low-level operating system primitives.

DEV Community

kubelet: Node Daemon

A systemd service acting as the cluster’s node agent. It watches the API server for pods assigned to its node.

Medium

  • SyncLoop: kubelet’s core event loop multiplexes changes from three channels: file updates, HTTP endpoints, and the API server watch stream.
  • PLEG (Pod Lifecycle Event Generator): Periodically polls the container runtime and translates raw OS process states into unified Pod lifecycle events.
  • CAdvisor: Gathers node- and container-level resource statistics (CPU, memory, network, disk) and exposes them to metrics endpoints.

Container Runtime Interface (CRI)

kubelet does not manage Linux namespaces or cgroups directly; it communicates over a local Unix domain socket using gRPC with a CRI-compliant runtime (like containerd or CRI-O). CRI breaks into two distinct services:

  • ImageService: Pulls images, unpacks root filesystems, and manages storage layers. Medium
  • RuntimeService: Handles container and pod sandbox lifecycles. Medium

Under the hood:

  1. containerd calls an OCI runtime (e.g., runc, crun).
  2. The runtime configures Linux kernel primitives:
    • Namespaces: pid, net, ipc, mnt, uts, user to isolate system resources.
      • Cgroups (v2): Restricts memory limits, CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) CPU quotas, and I/O pressure.
      • Pivot_root / OverlayFS: Mounts the container’s isolated root filesystem layers.

Pod Sandbox & The pause Container

Every pod begins by launching an infrastructure container (the pause container). The pause container makes a clone() syscall with new network and IPC namespace flags, and then sleeps indefinitely via pause(). All application containers in that pod join the pause container’s network namespace via setns(). This allows all containers within the pod to communicate over localhost and share the same IP address.

VMware

3. Networking Internals

Kubernetes enforces three invariants:

  1. Every pod gets its own unique, routable IP address. VMware
  2. Pods can communicate with all other pods across nodes without NAT.
  3. Agents on a host can communicate with all pods on that host.

Container Network Interface (CNI)

When a pod sandbox is created, kubelet delegates network creation to the CNI plugin (e.g., Cilium, Calico, Flannel).

  1. The CNI plugin creates a Virtual Ethernet pair (veth).
  2. It pushes one end into the pod’s network namespace (renamed to eth0) and anchors the other end in the host root network namespace (e.g., veth1234).
  3. It assigns an IP address to the pod’s eth0 via an IPAM (IP Address Management) plugin. VMware
  4. It sets up cross-node routing using either Overlay networks (VXLAN/Geneve tunneling encapsulation) or Direct Routing / BGP (programming the host route tables or upstream top-of-rack switches).

kube-proxy & Service Abstraction

A Service is not a process; it is a static Virtual IP (ClusterIP) fronting dynamic Pod IPs. kube-proxy watches Service and Endpoints/EndpointSlice objects, implementing traffic forwarding using one of three backends:

Medium - Medium

Proxy Mode Implementation Mechanism Characteristics
iptables Generates chains inside Netfilter nat tables using PREROUTING and OUTPUT hooks. Random probability-based matching (-m statistic --mode random). O(n)O(n)O(n) sequential chain evaluation causes latency spikes at thousands of services.
IPVS Kernel-space transport-layer load balancer utilizing hash tables inside Netfilter hooks. O(1)O(1)O(1) lookup performance, supports round-robin, least-connection, and session-affinity balancing algorithms.
eBPF (Cilium) Replaces kube-proxy entirely by attaching BPF programs to tc (Traffic Control) or socket layers (sock_ops). Bypasses core Netfilter connection tracking (conntrack), translating service VIPs to pod endpoints directly at the socket level.

4. End-to-End Walkthrough: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

To see how all components coordinate in real time, trace the lifecycle of a Deployment:

  1. Submission: kubectl sends an HTTP POST with the Deployment manifest to kube-apiserver.
  2. Admission & Persistence: kube-apiserver authenticates the token, checks RBAC permissions, runs mutating webhooks, validates the spec, writes the object to etcd, and acknowledges the client.
  3. Deployment Controller: The DeploymentController detects the new resource via its watch cache and creates a corresponding ReplicaSet.
  4. ReplicaSet Controller: The ReplicaSetController notices the missing replicas and writes new Pod specs with empty spec.nodeName fields.
  5. Scheduling: kube-scheduler filters out invalid nodes, scores remaining candidates, and executes a binding call setting spec.nodeName = "node-1".
  6. Execution (Kubelet): The kubelet on node-1 picks up the binding event via its watch stream:
    • Calls the container runtime via CRI to spawn the pause container.
      • Invokes the CNI plugin to configure interfaces, routing, and IP assignments.
      • Pulls application container images, sets cgroups and namespace restrictions, and starts the workload.
      • Reports container status back to the API server.
  7. Service Ingress: If a Service exposes the Deployment, kube-proxy on every node detects the pod’s new IP and updates the local routing tables (iptables/IPVS/eBPF maps).

Gemini said

In Kubernetes, an Object is a persistent entity in etcd that represents the intent of the cluster (its desired state) alongside its current status. Objects belong to specific API Groups and are split by scope: Namespaced (isolated to an environment) or Cluster-scoped (global infrastructure).

1. Workload Objects (Compute & Lifecycles)

These objects dictate how, where, and for how long your containerized workloads execute.

Kubernetes

  • Pod: The atomic deployable unit in Kubernetes. A wrapper around one or more tightly coupled containers that share IPC, Linux namespaces, and an IP address via a shared network namespace. Kubernetes
  • ReplicaSet: Ensures a specified number of identical Pod replicas remain running at all times. Uses set-based label selectors to acquire or evict running Pods.
  • Deployment: A declarative supervisor over ReplicaSets. Manages rolling updates, rollbacks, and zero-downtime version transitions for stateless workloads.
  • StatefulSet: Manages stateful applications (e.g., databases, distributed stores). Provides stable, persistent network identifiers (e.g., db-0, db-1), ordered deployment/termination, and automated provisioning of dedicated storage volumes per replica. Kubernetes+ 1
  • DaemonSet: Guarantees that a copy of a specific Pod runs on all (or targeted) nodes. Commonly used for host log collectors, metrics scrapers, and storage or CNI network daemons. Kubernetes
  • Job: Supervises batch processes designed to run to completion rather than stay up continuously. Retries failing pods until a specified number of successful completions is reached. Kubernetes
  • CronJob: A time-based scheduler (cron syntax) that instantiates Job objects at designated intervals or deadlines.

2. Discovery, Routing & Networking Objects

These resources stitch dynamic, ephemeral pod IPs together into static network endpoints and handle inbound ingress.

Kubernetes

  • Service: An abstraction defining a logical set of Pods and a consistent policy to access them.
    • ClusterIP: Virtual IP accessible only internally inside the cluster.
      • NodePort: Exposes the Service on a static port across every node’s external IP.
      • LoadBalancer: Provisions an external cloud-provider load balancer routing to the NodePort/Pods.
      • Headless (clusterIP: None): Returns direct Pod IPs via DNS A/AAAA records for direct peer discovery.
  • Endpoints / EndpointSlice: The dynamic address book behind a Service. Contains the actual IP and port tuples of healthy Pods matching the Service’s selector. EndpointSlice splits large lists into chunks (default 100 endpoints) to avoid control plane serialization bottlenecks.
  • Ingress: Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) routing rules (host, path, TLS termination) mapping inbound external requests to internal Services. Implemented by an Ingress Controller (e.g., NGINX, Envoy).
  • Gateway API (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute): The modern, expressive, role-oriented successor to Ingress. Decouples infrastructure provisioning (cluster ops) from route matching and traffic splitting (app developers).
  • NetworkPolicy: Firewall rules enforced at the CNI layer. Dictates ingress and egress packet filtering for Pods based on IP CIDRs, namespaces, and pod labels.

3. Configuration & Secrets Objects

Used to inject operational variables, configs, and credentials without rebuilding container images.

  • ConfigMap: Key-value store for non-confidential configuration data (environment variables, config files, command-line arguments) mounted as files or injected as environment variables.
  • Secret: Stores sensitive data (keys, certificates, passwords) encoded in Base64. Can be mounted as memory-backed tmpfs volumes to prevent secrets from touching node disks.

4. Storage Objects

Abstracts physical disk volumes (cloud block stores, NFS, local NVMe) into portable cluster assets.

  • PersistentVolume (PV): A piece of networked storage in the cluster provisioned by an administrator or dynamically through a StorageClass. Cluster-scoped.
  • PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC): A request for storage by a user (specifying access modes, size, and StorageClass). Namespaced. Bound 1:1 with an appropriate PV.
  • StorageClass: Defines storage dynamic provisioning parameters (provisioner plugin, volume type, IOPS tier, reclaim policies such as Delete or Retain).
  • VolumeAttachment: Tracks the attaching of a CSI (Container Storage Interface) volume to a specific worker node.
  • CSIDriver & CSINode: Cluster-level metadata specifying installed third-party storage drivers and node-specific discovery details.

5. Cluster Topology & Administrative Objects

Resources that partition the cluster, describe machines, and coordinate leases.

  • Namespace: Virtual clusters backed by a single physical cluster, providing scoping for object names, RBAC boundaries, and resource quotas.
  • Node: Represents a physical machine or VM in the cluster, registering allocatable CPU/memory, kernel version, condition heartbeats, and taints.
  • Lease: Lightweight coordination primitives inside the coordination.k8s.io group. Used by control plane components for leader election and by Kubelets to publish node health heartbeats.
  • ResourceQuota: Sets hard upper bounds on total resource consumption (CPU, memory, object counts) within a single Namespace.
  • LimitRange: Enforces min/max resource constraints and default resource requests/limits for individual containers inside a Namespace.

6. Security, Identity & Access Control (RBAC)

Objects governing authentication, authorization, and process-level privilege escalation.

  • ServiceAccount: Identity assigned to processes running inside Pods to authenticate against the kube-apiserver.
  • Role / ClusterRole: Sets of additive permissions (get, list, watch, create, etc.) on API resources. Role is namespaced; ClusterRole applies globally across all namespaces.
  • RoleBinding / ClusterRoleBinding: Grants the permissions defined in a Role/ClusterRole to a subject (User, Group, or ServiceAccount).
  • PodDisruptionBudget (PDB): Defines the minimum available or maximum unavailable replicas during voluntary disruptions (e.g., node drain, maintenance updates).
  • CertificateSigningRequest (CSR): Used to request X.509 client/server certificates signed by the cluster’s internal Certificate Authority (CA).

7. Extensibility & Dynamic Admission

Objects that allow extending the Kubernetes API schema and intercepting requests at runtime.

  • CustomResourceDefinition (CRD): Extends the Kubernetes API by defining new custom object kinds, schemas (OpenAPI v3), and endpoints without modifying core code. Kubernetes
  • MutatingWebhookConfiguration: Directs kube-apiserver to call external HTTP services to modify objects prior to persistence (e.g., auto-injecting monitoring agents).
  • ValidatingWebhookConfiguration: Directs kube-apiserver to evaluate objects against external admission webhooks, accepting or rejecting payloads based on organization policy.

Summary Reference Table

Functional Domain Primary Kubernetes Objects Scope
Workloads Pod, Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob Namespaced
Networking Service, Endpoints, EndpointSlice, Ingress, NetworkPolicy, HTTPRoute Namespaced
Configuration ConfigMap, Secret Namespaced
Storage (User) PersistentVolumeClaim Namespaced
Storage (Infra) PersistentVolume, StorageClass, CSIDriver, VolumeAttachment Cluster
Cluster & Identity Namespace, Node, ServiceAccount, Role, RoleBinding, ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding Mixed
Governance & Limits ResourceQuota, LimitRange, PodDisruptionBudget Namespaced
Extensions CustomResourceDefinition, MutatingWebhookConfiguration, ValidatingWebhookConfiguration Cluster

item.title: Latency numbers
item.description:
The classic list originally popularized by Jeff Dean (and later expanded by Peter Norvig and Colin Scott) provides essential orders of magnitude for systems engineering and performance estimation.

GitHub Gist

1. Canonical Latency Numbers

Operation Latency Standard Representation
L1 cache reference 0.5 – 1 ns ~1 ns
Branch mispredict 3 – 5 ns ~3–5 ns
L2 cache reference 3 – 7 ns ~4–7 ns
Mutex lock / unlock 15 – 25 ns ~20 ns
Main memory reference (RAM) 50 – 100 ns ~100 ns
Compress 1 KB with Snappy/Zippy 2,000 – 3,000 ns ~2–3 µs
Send 2 KB over 10 Gbps network ~1,600 ns ~1.6 µs
Send 1 KB over 1 Gbps network 10,000 ns 10 µs
SSD random read (4 KB, NVMe/PCIe) 10,000 – 100,000 ns 10 – 100 µs
Read 1 MB sequentially from memory 3,000 – 10,000 ns (modern) 250,000 ns (classic) 10 – 250 µs
Round trip in same datacenter 500,000 ns 0.5 ms
Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD 200,000 – 1,000,000 ns 0.2 – 1 ms
HDD seek time (rotational latency + arm) 2,000,000 – 10,000,000 ns 2 – 10 ms
Read 1 MB sequentially from HDD 5,000,000 – 20,000,000 ns 5 – 20 ms
Cross-continental packet round trip (e.g., US to Europe) 150,000,000 ns 150 ms

2. Scaled to Human Time (1 CPU Cycle ≈ 1 Second)

Scaling 0.5–1 ns to ~1 second highlights the stark gaps across the hardware hierarchy:

Operation Actual Time Scaled Time Real-World Analogy
L1 cache hit 0.5 – 1 ns 1 second Grabbing a piece of paper on your desk
L2 cache hit ~4 ns 4 seconds Grabbing a book from a shelf within reach
RAM access ~100 ns 1.5 minutes Walking down the hall to fetch a file
NVMe SSD random read ~20 µs ~5.5 hours A half-day road trip
Same-datacenter network RTT ~500 µs ~5.8 days Taking a week off
HDD seek ~10 ms ~4 months A semester abroad
Transatlantic packet RTT ~150 ms ~5 years Completing an entire degree

3. Rules of Thumb for System Design

  1. Avoid Random Disk I/O: Sequential throughput on disk and flash is orders of magnitude faster than random seeks. Google SRE
  2. Datacenter vs. WAN Boundaries: In-rack or same-datacenter communication (~0.5 ms) allows ~2,000 round trips/sec, whereas cross-continent WAN round trips (~150 ms) max out at 6–7 trips/sec. Google SRE
  3. RAM Is Fast, but Cache Locality Still Dominates: A single cache miss that hits main memory takes ~100× longer than an L1 cache hit. Data-oriented layout (contiguous arrays, avoiding pointer chasing) maximizes hardware prefetching and cache line utilization.

item.title: Docker internals and runc
item.description:
At the Linux kernel level, there is no discrete entity called a “container.” A container is simply a standard Linux process isolated by namespaces, resource-constrained by cgroups, bound to a dedicated root filesystem using chroot/pivot_root, and restricted by security mechanisms like seccomp and capabilities.

The Runtime Architecture: Docker to runc

Running docker run triggers a chain of components adhering to Open Container Initiative (OCI) standards:

  1. Docker CLI / Engine (dockerd): Accepts the client request, manages local storage, interacts with image registries, unpacks image layers, and calls containerd over a gRPC API.
  2. containerd: Manages the container lifecycle, image distribution, and snapshot storage. When told to create a container, it delegates the low-level execution to a runtime shim (containerd-shim).
  3. containerd-shim: Sits between containerd and the low-level runtime. It holds the standard I/O (stdin/stdout/stderr) pipes and file descriptors open, reports exit statuses, and prevents the container from dying if dockerd or containerd crashes or restarts.
  4. runc: The OCI reference implementation. It reads an OCI bundle (a directory containing a rootfs filesystem and a JSON configuration file called config.json), makes the low-level Linux syscalls to configure the isolation environment, launches the containerized process, and immediately exits, leaving the process running under the shim.

The Core Linux Primitives

1. Linux Namespaces (What the Process Can See)

Namespaces partition kernel resources so that a process inside a namespace sees its own isolated instance of global resources. When runc initializes a container, it uses the clone() system call with specific flags, or joins existing namespaces using unshare() and setns().

  • PID (Process IDs): The container process becomes PID 1 inside its own namespace, handling signals and child reaping, while retaining a regular PID on the host.
  • NET (Network Devices & Routing): Isolates network interfaces, IP routing tables, firewall rules, and ports. Usually paired with a virtual Ethernet pair (veth), linking the container’s network stack to a host bridge (docker0).
  • MNT (Mount Points): Provides an isolated filesystem mount table. Mounts and unmounts inside the container do not affect the host.
  • IPC (Inter-Process Communication): Isolates System V IPC and POSIX message queues.
  • UTS (Hostnames): Allows the container to define its own hostname and domain name without modifying the host system.
  • USER (UID and GID Mappings): Maps host user and group IDs to different IDs inside the namespace (e.g., UID 1000 on the host can act as UID 0/root inside the container for rootless execution).
  • CGROUP (Cgroup Root): Masks the host’s actual cgroup directory tree structure from the process.

2. Control Groups / cgroups (What the Process Can Use)

While namespaces restrict visibility, cgroups restrict and account for hardware resource usage.

  • Resource Limiting: Caps how much memory, CPU quota, block I/O bandwidth, and network priority a group of processes can consume.
  • Accounting & Metrics: Tracks usage (e.g., reporting memory pressure and page cache consumption).
  • Process Number Limits (pids controller): Prevents fork bombs by capping the total number of processes inside the container.
  • OOM Handling: When a container exceeds its memory hard limit, the kernel’s Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer selectively terminates processes within that cgroup rather than bringing down host processes.

Linux environments predominantly use cgroups v2, which features a unified hierarchy where a single process tree controls all resource controllers simultaneously (unlike cgroups v1, which had separate trees for memory, cpu, and blkio).

3. Root Filesystems and Layering: OverlayFS & pivot_root

Containers do not boot a kernel; they reuse the host kernel with an independent directory tree:

  • Layering via OverlayFS: Docker images consist of immutable read-only layers. OverlayFS stacks these layers (lowerdir) with an ephemeral read-write upper layer (upperdir) and presents them as a single unified view (merged). Changes made inside the container write only to the upperdir via copy-on-write (CoW).
  • pivot_root vs chroot: While chroot changes the apparent root directory for the current process, it has well-known escape paths (especially for processes with root privileges). runc mounts the container’s root filesystem and uses pivot_root(new_root, put_old). This system call moves the current root mount to a temporary directory inside the new root, swaps in the new root, and then unmounts the old host root—making escape from the mount namespace impossible via directory traversal.

4. Security Isolation: Capabilities & Seccomp

A root user (UID 0) inside a traditional container could theoretically control hardware or manipulate kernel modules if unrestricted. Two mechanisms strip dangerous abilities:

  • Linux Capabilities: Breaks traditional root authority into granular privileges (e.g., CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_CHOWN). runc drops most dangerous capabilities by default, such as CAP_SYS_ADMIN (mounting filesystems, loading BPF programs) and CAP_SYS_MODULE (loading kernel modules).
  • Seccomp (Secure Computing Mode): Acts as a syscall firewall. The default Docker seccomp profile filters roughly 44 out of over 400 system calls (blocking syscalls like reboot, kexec_load, mount, and sys_chroot).

Step-by-Step Execution Inside runc 

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1. Read OCI bundle config.json & prepare rootfs |
+------------------------------+------------------------------+
|
v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| 2. clone() child process with CLONE_NEW* namespace flags |
+------------------------------+------------------------------+
|
v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| 3. Attach child to cgroup paths in /sys/fs/cgroup |
+------------------------------+------------------------------+
|
v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| 4. pivot_root() into the new rootfs & unmount old host root |
+------------------------------+------------------------------+
|
v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| 5. Drop Linux capabilities & load Seccomp BPF filter |
+------------------------------+------------------------------+
|
v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| 6. execve() replaces runc child with the target app binary |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Once execve() executes, the child process is running your container application in-place under the configured boundaries, while the parent runc process exits.

item.title: HTTP
item.description:
The evolution across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 reflects a continuous push to eliminate latency, reduce network round-trips, and overcome transmission bottlenecks across the web.

HTTP/1.1 (1997 / 1999) — The Text-Based Baseline

HTTP/1.1 standardized modern web semantics (verbs like GET, POST, status codes, headers, and caching directives) and introduced key persistence improvements over HTTP/1.0.

  • Underlying Transport: Plain TCP (Layer 4).
  • Format: Human-readable ASCII text headers and messages separated by CRLF (\r\n).
  • Key Innovations:
    • Persistent Connections (Keep-Alive by default): Allows multiple request/response cycles over a single TCP connection, avoiding repeated 3-way TCP handshakes.
      • Chunked Transfer Encoding: Allows streaming responses of unknown initial payload size using chunk headers.
      • Pipelining: Clients could send multiple requests back-to-back without waiting for responses, though rarely deployed due to intermediary proxy bugs.
  • The Core Bottleneck — Application Head-of-Line (HoL) Blocking:
    • HTTP/1.1 enforces strict FIFO ordering per TCP connection. If Request #1 stalls on the server (e.g., waiting on a slow database query), Request #2 and #3 queued behind it must wait, even if ready to deliver.
      • Browsers worked around this by opening 6 parallel TCP connections per host domain, introducing significant socket, handshake, and TLS negotiation overhead.

HTTP/2 (2015) — Multiplexing Over a Single Connection

HTTP/2 retained HTTP/1.1 request/response semantics (GET, POST, headers, status codes) while completely overhauling the wire format and framing mechanism to eliminate application-layer HoL blocking.

  • Underlying Transport: TCP + TLS (Layer 4). In practice, HTTP/2 is almost universally deployed over encrypted TLS (h2).
  • Format: Strict Binary Framing Layer. Every message is split into typed binary frames (HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS, RST_STREAM, etc.).
  • Key Innovations:
    • True Stream Multiplexing: Multiple bidirectional streams interleave independently over a single TCP connection. Packets from Stream 1, Stream 3, and Stream 5 can be sent concurrently without waiting for Stream 1 to complete.
      • HPACK Header Compression: HTTP headers are statefully compressed via pre-indexed static tables and dynamically synchronized differential tables between client and server, dramatically reducing redundant header overhead across requests.
      • Stream Prioritization & Flow Control: Allows the client to signal resource weight/dependency (e.g., render-blocking CSS prioritized over footer images).
      • Server Push: Allowed servers to pre-emptively push assets to the client cache (though deprecated in modern browsers due to cache invalidation complexity).
  • The Remaining Bottleneck — TCP-Level Head-of-Line Blocking:
    • Because all logical streams share one OS-level TCP socket, TCP’s byte-stream guarantees enforce strict packet order. If a single IP packet drops, the OS TCP receiver buffer freezes all HTTP/2 streams on that connection until the lost segment is retransmitted. Under high packet loss (>2%), HTTP/2 can perform worse than multi-connection HTTP/1.1.

HTTP/3 (2022) — Transport Reinvention Over QUIC

HTTP/3 completely decouples HTTP from traditional TCP, replacing TCP and TLS with QUIC (a user-space, transport-layer protocol running on top of UDP).

  • Underlying Transport: QUIC over UDP (Layer 4).
  • Format: Binary frames mapped directly to QUIC stream primitives.
  • Key Innovations:
    • Zero Transport HoL Blocking: QUIC implements streams natively in transport logic. If a packet belonging to Stream A drops on the wire, only Stream A pauses. Stream B, Stream C, and Stream D continue streaming to the application without interruption.
      • Integrated TLS 1.3 Encryption: Encryption is baked directly into QUIC’s transport layer rather than sitting on top. Handshake round-trips drop to 1-RTT on first connection and 0-RTT on resumption (data sent alongside the initial connection frame).
      • Connection Migration via Connection IDs: TCP connections are bound to a 4-tuple (Src IP, Src Port, Dst IP, Dst Port). Switching from Wi-Fi to cellular breaks TCP connections. QUIC uses a random 64-bit Connection ID independent of IP/port, allowing persistent connections to survive network network handoffs seamlessly without re-handshaking.
      • QPACK Header Compression: A redesign of HPACK that handles unordered packet arrivals across streams without causing transport stalls.

Structural Comparison

Feature HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3
Underlying Layer 4 TCP TCP QUIC (over UDP)
Framing Format Plain ASCII Text Binary Frames Binary Frames (via QUIC)
Multiplexing No (FIFO per connection) Yes (Application-layer) Yes (Transport-native)
Head-of-Line Blocking At Application layer At TCP transport layer None
Header Compression None HPACK QPACK
Handshake Latency 2–3 RTTs (TCP + TLS) 2–3 RTTs (TCP + TLS) 0–1 RTT (QUIC + TLS 1.3)
Connection Migration Fails on IP/network change Fails on IP/network change Native via Connection ID

item.title: Linux boot process
item.description:
The Linux boot process follows a deterministic sequence transitioning hardware execution from firmware, through low-level CPU modes and memory staging, up to the first user-space process.

1

Firmware Initialization (BIOS / UEFI)

1.Firmware Initialization (BIOS / UEFI):

  • Power-On Self-Test (POST): The processor begins executing code at the reset vector (0xFFFFFFF0 on x86/x64). Firmware tests hardware peripherals, discovers system RAM, and initializes basic bus topology.
  • Handover:
    • Legacy BIOS: Searches configured boot disks for an active partition containing a 512-byte Master Boot Record (MBR) at sector 0 and loads it into memory at 0x7C00.
    • Modern UEFI: Reads the GUID Partition Table (GPT), accesses the FAT-formatted EFI System Partition (ESP), and executes a pre-configured architecture-specific EFI binary (e.g., /EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI or grubx64.efi).

2

Bootloader Execution (GRUB 2)

2.Bootloader Execution (GRUB 2):

  • Stage 1 & Stage 1.5: Under BIOS, Stage 1 (MBR) loads Stage 1.5 / core.img embedded in the unpartitioned space between MBR and the first sector. Under UEFI, the firmware directly executes grubx64.efi.
  • Stage 2: Loads filesystem drivers (ext4, btrfs, xfs), parses /boot/grub/grub.cfg, displays the boot menu, and handles kernel command-line parameters.
  • Kernel & Initramfs Placement: Loads the compressed kernel image (vmlinuz) and initial RAM filesystem (initramfs or initrd) into physical RAM, transitions the CPU from real mode / protected mode to 64-bit long mode, and jumps to the kernel entry point.

3

Kernel Startup & Hardware Probing

3.Kernel Startup & Hardware Probing:

  • Decompression & Memory Setup: The kernel self-extracts, maps memory pages, sets up page tables, enables paging, and initializes core data structures (IDT, GDT, scheduler).
  • Device Discovery: Identifies CPU topology, NUMA nodes, interrupts (APIC), and probes PCI/PCIe buses.
  • Driver & Subsystem Bringup: Initializes core subsystems including memory management, timer ticks, virtual filesystem (VFS), and IPC.

4

Initramfs Staging (Early Userspace)

4.Initramfs Staging (Early Userspace):

  • Temporary Root: The kernel mounts initramfs as a temporary root filesystem (tmpfs) in memory and executes /init (typically a minimal shell or systemd instance).
  • Storage Modules: Loads specialized storage drivers not compiled statically into the kernel—such as device mappers for LUKS disk encryption, software RAID (mdadm), LVM volumes, or network root mounts (iSCSI, NFS).
  • Switch Root: Mounts the real root filesystem (/) from persistent storage (read-only initially), moves mount points, and runs switch_root / pivot_root to wipe the temporary RAM filesystem and hand control to the permanent filesystem.

5

Initialization System (systemd / PID 1)

5.Initialization System (systemd / PID 1):

  • First Userspace Process: The kernel executes /sbin/init (symlinked to /usr/lib/systemd/systemd on modern distributions), assigning it PID 1.
  • Target Traversal: Reads dependency graphs defined in unit files, resolving boot targets (e.g., sysinit.target →\to→ basic.target →\to→ multi-user.target / graphical.target).
  • Mounts & Daemons: Re-mounts the root filesystem read-write, mounts /etc/fstab entries, initializes device nodes via systemd-udevd, sets hostname and networking, and spawns background system daemons in parallel.
  • Display & Login: Launches the display manager (gdm, sddm) or virtual terminal login prompts (agetty), completing the boot pipeline.

item.title: Linux file system
item.description:
In Linux, everything is treated as a file—including directories, hardware devices, and network sockets—organized under a single, unified hierarchical tree starting at the root directory (/).

Unlike Windows, which uses separate drive letters (C:\, D:\), Linux mounts all physical drives, partitions, and external media into specific branches of this single directory tree according to the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS).

Linux Directory Hierarchy Structure. Source: Made with Google AI

Core Directory Breakdown

Directory Purpose Typical Contents
/ Root directory Top level of the filesystem; everything starts here.
/bin Essential user binaries Core commands needed for single-user mode and booting (ls, cp, bash, cat).
/sbin System binaries Administrative commands reserved for root/system recovery (iptables, fdisk, reboot).
/etc System configuration Machine-local host configuration files and startup scripts (fstab, passwd, nginx/).
/home User personal files Stores personal directories (/home/username) for documents, downloads, and user settings.
/root Root user home The dedicated home directory for the superuser (root).
/var Variable data Files that grow dynamically during runtime (logs in /var/log, mail spools, databases).
/tmp Temporary files Volatile scratch space; usually cleared automatically on reboot.
/usr User system resources Read-only user data, second-tier binaries (/usr/bin), libraries (/usr/lib), and docs.
/opt Optional software Third-party or self-contained application packages (e.g., Google Chrome, proprietary tools).
/dev Device nodes Special files representing hardware devices (disks like sda, terminals like tty, /dev/null).
/proc & /sys Virtual filesystems Dynamic runtime metadata exposed by the kernel; exists in RAM rather than disk.
/mnt & /media Mount points Temporary mount points (/mnt for manual mounts, /media for auto-mounted USB/removable drives).

Key Concepts

  • Everything is a File: Linux interfaces with hardware and processes using file descriptors. Reading from /dev/urandom produces random bytes; writing to /dev/null discards data.
  • Inodes (Index Nodes): Disk storage separates file metadata from file content. An inode stores file type, permissions, size, timestamps, and data block locations. The directory entry simply maps a human-readable filename to an inode number.
  • Permissions & Ownership: Every file belongs to an owner and a group, carrying read (r), write (w), and execute (x) permissions evaluated across three tiers: User, Group, and Others.
  • Underlying Filesystems: While the directory tree provides a standard logical view, Linux formats storage using specialized filesystems such as ext4 (default standard), XFS (high-throughput, large data), and Btrfs or ZFS (snapshots, volume management).

item.title: Networks
item.description:
The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model is a conceptual framework standardized by the ISO that partitions network communication into seven distinct abstraction layers, standardizing how data moves from physical hardware up to end-user software applications.

The 7-layer OSI reference architecture. Source: Maccow Creatives / Getty Images

Layer 1: Physical Layer

Transmits unstructured raw bit streams over a physical transmission medium (electrical voltages, radio frequencies, optical pulses). It defines pinouts, cable specifications, signaling rates, and physical connectors.

  • Protocol Data Unit (PDU): Bit
  • Hardware: Hubs, repeaters, network cables (Cat6, fiber optics), transceivers
  • Protocols & Standards:
    • Ethernet physical layer (IEEE 802.3 PHY): 10BASE-T, 100BASE-TX, 1000BASE-T
      • Wireless PHY standards: IEEE 802.11a/b/g/n/ac/ax (physical modulation layers)
      • Serial & Telephony: RS-232, RS-485, V.35, T1/E1, ISDN (Layer 1 specs)
      • Optical Transport: SONET/SDH, OTN (G.709)
      • Broadband access: DSL, DOCSIS (PHY specs)

Layer 2: Data Link Layer

Provides node-to-node data transfer across the same physical segment, handles physical addressing (MAC addresses), framing, error detection (CRC/FCS), and flow control. Often subdivided into Media Access Control (MAC) and Logical Link Control (LLC).

  • Protocol Data Unit (PDU): Frame
  • Hardware: Layer 2 switches, network interface cards (NICs), bridges
  • Protocols & Standards:
    • LAN: Ethernet (IEEE 802.3 MAC), Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11 MAC), Token Ring (IEEE 802.5)
      • WAN & Point-to-Point: PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol), HDLC, Frame Relay, ATM
      • Switching & Redundancy: STP (IEEE 802.1D Spanning Tree Protocol), RSTP, VLAN tagging (IEEE 802.1Q)
      • Tunneling & Link Layer Control: L2TP, PPPoE, ARP* (Address Resolution Protocol operates across Layer 2 and Layer 3 boundaries to map IPs to MACs)

Layer 3: Network Layer

Handles host-to-host addressing across different networks, path determination, and packet routing. It abstracts network topologies so data can traverse multiple intermediate hops.

  • Protocol Data Unit (PDU): Packet
  • Hardware: Routers, Layer 3 switches
  • Protocols & Standards:
    • Addressing & Delivery: IPv4, IPv6
      • Control & Diagnostics: ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), ICMPv6, IGMP (multicast group management)
      • Routing Protocols (Interior): OSPF, IS-IS, RIP, EIGRP
      • Routing Protocols (Exterior): BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)
      • Network Security & Tunneling: IPsec (AH, ESP), GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation)

Layer 4: Transport Layer

Responsible for end-to-end communication between application processes on host devices. It manages multiplexing/demultiplexing via port numbers, segmentation, reassembly, error correction, and flow/congestion control.

  • Protocol Data Unit (PDU): Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP)
  • Protocols & Standards:
    • TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): Connection-oriented, ordered byte-stream delivery with congestion and flow control
      • UDP (User Datagram Protocol): Connectionless, lightweight, low-latency datagram delivery without retransmission
      • SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol): Multi-stream, message-oriented transport protocol with multi-homing support
      • QUIC: UDP-based transport protocol incorporating integrated TLS 1.3 encryption and multiplexing
      • DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol): Unreliable datagram transport with congestion notification

Layer 5: Session Layer

Establishes, manages, synchronizes, and terminates communication sessions (dialogues) between applications. It controls full-duplex or half-duplex operations and inserts checkpoints for session recovery.

  • Protocol Data Unit (PDU): Data
  • Protocols & Standards:
    • RPC (Remote Procedure Call): Manages client-server procedural interactions
      • NetBIOS: Session establishment between computers on a LAN
      • PPTP (Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol): Encapsulates and manages tunneling sessions
      • SMPP (Short Message Peer-to-Peer): Exchanges SMS messages between SMSCs and messaging systems
      • SIP (Session Initiation Protocol): Signaling protocol for setting up and tearing down multimedia/VoIP sessions
      • Sockets API / Named Pipes: OS abstractions managing local and remote communication sessions

Layer 6: Presentation Layer

Translates, formats, encrypts, and compresses data so that application-layer entities exchange readable information regardless of internal representations (e.g., character encoding, byte ordering).

  • Protocol Data Unit (PDU): Data
  • Protocols & Standards:
    • Encryption & Security Handshakes: TLS / SSL (presentation functions: negotiation of cipher suites, encryption/decryption)
      • Data Representation & Serialization: ASN.1, XDR (External Data Representation), JSON, Protocol Buffers, MessagePack
      • Character Encoding: ASCII, UTF-8, UTF-16, EBCDIC
      • Media Compression & Encoding: JPEG, PNG, GIF, MPEG, H.264, MP3

Layer 7: Application Layer

Directly interacts with software applications to provide end-user network services, resource discovery, authentication, and application messaging.

  • Protocol Data Unit (PDU): Data
  • Protocols & Standards:
    • Web: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3
      • File Transfer: FTP, SFTP, TFTP, NFS, SMB/CIFS
      • Email & Messaging: SMTP, IMAP, POP3, XMPP
      • Network Management & Directory: DNS, DHCP, SNMP, LDAP, NTP (Network Time Protocol)
      • Remote Shell & Terminal: SSH, Telnet

Layer Summary Matrix

# Layer Primary Function Addressing / Identifier Key Protocols
7 Application Network services for user applications URLs, URIs, FQDNs HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH, DHCP
6 Presentation Formatting, encryption, serialization Data syntax / schemas TLS/SSL, ASN.1, JSON, XDR
5 Session Dialogue control & session lifecycle Session IDs, RPC handles SIP, NetBIOS, RPC, SMPP
4 Transport End-to-end delivery & port multiplexing Port numbers (0–65535) TCP, UDP, QUIC, SCTP
3 Network Routing & logical addressing IP addresses IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, OSPF, BGP
2 Data Link Framing, local MAC addressing & error checks MAC addresses, VLAN tags Ethernet, Wi-Fi, PPP, ARP
1 Physical Physical transmission of raw bits Voltage, wavelength, pins 1000BASE-T, RS-232, 802.11 PHY
